lesson.menu_title: Must, Required, Obligated -- Compliance and Governance
lesson.menu_desc: The language of rules: must, be required to, must not and do not have to, plus the words of governance -- governance, policy, code of conduct, mandatory, disclosure, conflict of interest, due diligence, breach, oversight, whistleblower
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 33 -- Must, Required, Obligated
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Maria Claudia Curimbaba | Lesson 33 -- Must, Required, Obligated
lesson.grammar_point: obligation, prohibition and lack of obligation (must / be required to / must not / do not have to / had to)

listenings.text: When I tell people I work in compliance, they usually think of a long list of things they are not allowed to do. I understand why. But that is not what the rules are for. The rules protect the honest people in the company. If there is a clear policy on gifts, an honest manager does not have to decide alone, at a dinner, whether a present is too expensive. The policy has already decided for him. So I ask every new manager to remember only one rule, even if they forget everything else. If you are not sure, you must ask before you act, not after. Asking before costs five minutes. Explaining after can cost a career.

A few years ago a supplier sent me an expensive watch, the week after we signed a contract with them. My first thought was that it was not a problem. The contract was already signed, so the gift could not change my decision. That was wrong. Our policy said that managers must not accept gifts above one hundred dollars, at any time. There was no exception for after the signature. A colleague saw the box on my desk and asked me about it. In the end I had to return the watch, and I was required to disclose it to the audit committee. Nobody punished me. But I learned that a rule does not ask what you were thinking. It asks what you did.

extra_audio.text: First, you check the policy to see if the sponsorship needs an approval. Then, you do your due diligence on the partner before you sign anything. After that, every manager discloses any conflict of interest before the vote. Next, the board votes, and nobody with a conflict votes on that point. Finally, you keep a written record, so that the audit committee has oversight of the payment.
